[SYNTHETIC FIXTURE] Protein language model features enable binding specificity prediction for unseen transcription factors

This document is a synthetic test fixture for the CDRI test-suite. It does not describe a real study; all numbers are invented for testing parsers and the reading ledger.

Abstract

Predicting the DNA-binding specificity of transcription factors (TFs) that were not seen during training is a central obstacle for sequence-to-function models. We condition a convolutional sequence model on embeddings of the TF DNA-binding domain produced by a protein language model, so that information about an unseen TF is carried by its descriptor rather than by a TF-specific output head. On a homology-aware split the model improves the median Spearman correlation over a nearest-neighbour baseline. We discuss when the descriptor is uninformative.

1 Introduction

Classical position weight matrices treat binding as an additive energy over positions and remain the reference representation of TF specificity. Deep sequence models improve in-distribution accuracy but are trained with one output per TF, which provides no mechanism to generalize to a TF without training data. Prior work shares a trunk across TFs but still requires labelled data for every new factor. We change the problem definition: the target is a function of both the DNA sequence and a descriptor of the protein, and generalization to unseen entities must come from the descriptor space.

2 Methods

2.1 Model

Let x denote a one-hot DNA sequence of length L and let z denote the mean-pooled protein language model embedding of the DNA-binding domain. A convolutional encoder produces position features h(x). The TF descriptor is mapped by a small network to feature-wise scale and shift parameters (FiLM conditioning), which modulate h(x) before global max pooling. The predicted binding score is (Eq. 1). The conditioning is the only path through which the identity of the TF enters the model.

2.2 Objective

Training minimizes a pairwise ranking loss over probes for each TF, (Eq. 2), so that only the within-TF ordering of probes is supervised. Scores are therefore not calibrated across TFs. We assume that binding preferences of homologous DNA-binding domains vary smoothly in embedding space.

2.3 Data and splits

Probe intensities are rank-normalized per experiment. TFs are clustered by DNA-binding domain family at 40 percent sequence identity and whole clusters are assigned to train, validation or test, so that test TFs have no close homolog in training. Hyperparameters: learning rate 0.001, batch size 256, 30 epochs, early stopping on validation Spearman.

3 Results

On held-out clusters the median per-TF Spearman correlation was 0.41 compared with 0.33 for nearest-neighbour transfer of the closest training TF's model (Table 2). Removing FiLM conditioning (concatenating z instead) reduced the median to 0.35 (ablation, Table 3). Performance decreased with distance to the nearest training TF and was close to the baseline for families with fewer than three training members. When the split was random instead of homology-aware the median rose to 0.58, indicating that random splits overstate unseen-TF generalization.

4 Discussion and Limitations

The descriptor carries information only within the support of the training families; TFs from families absent in training are predicted poorly. The ranking objective cannot estimate absolute affinities. The method assumes equilibrium-like binding measured in vitro and does not model cooperativity or chromatin context.

Supplementary Note 1: Additional analyses

We repeated the homology-aware evaluation with three random seeds; the median per-TF Spearman correlation varied between 0.40 and 0.42. We also evaluated a variant in which the descriptor was replaced by a random vector of the same dimension; performance dropped to the level of the nearest-neighbour baseline, which indicates that the gain depends on information in the descriptor rather than on additional parameters. Replicate experiments for the same TF agreed with a median Spearman correlation of 0.47, which bounds the achievable correlation on this assay. A calibration analysis across TFs was not performed because the objective only constrains within-TF ordering.
